entities.summary:
Louis de Sancerre (died February 6, 1402) emerged as a pivotal military commander and statesman for the French Crown during the latter stages of the Hundred Years' War, serving as Marshal of France from 1368 and later as Constable of France from 1397 until his death. His career spanned a critical period for the Valois dynasty, marked by efforts to consolidate royal authority and repel English incursions following the disastrous defeats earlier in the conflict. Sancerre's strategic acumen and unwavering loyalty made him a trusted lieutenant to King Charles V and, more importantly, a stabilizing force during the turbulent minority and early reign of Charles VI, profoundly influencing the direction of French military policy.

His military career began under Bertrand du Guesclin, where he honed his skills in guerrilla warfare and siegecraft. Sancerre distinguished himself in campaigns across France, notably in the reconquest of Poitou and Saintonge from English control in the 1370s. As Marshal, he led significant royal forces, participating in the critical Battle of Roosebeke in 1382 against the Flemish rebels, a decisive victory that reasserted French power in the Low Countries. His elevation to Constable of France, the supreme military commander, in 1397, following the disgrace of Olivier de Clisson, placed him at the apex of the French military hierarchy, where he continued to advocate for aggressive strategies against English holdings and contributed to maintaining internal order amidst growing factionalism within the French court.
